comments.text:
Josh Mandel, MD, from what I gather the adjudication step is the real, big contribution.

The forced evidence quote on both sides of each citation is the move that separates this from the last decade of role-classification work. It makes every edge in the graph auditable.

Worth flagging that this lands as a researcher tool, which is correct for the use case you built for. The interface you describe, bundle plus chat window, serves someone who can read the underlying papers and evaluate the adjudication.

An adjacent question is what a version looks like for the person downstream of all those citations, who receives the claim in a clinical encounter without the option to audit it themselves. Different output layer, same substrate.

The HCQ run and the 781 flagged invention patterns are the kind of artifact that changes what is possible for that downstream work. And a huge Thank You for shipping it open!

What does calibration against a held-out human coder look like when you get to it?

comments.text:
THIS IS SUPERB, Josh.  Is there any way to make it clean up the character codes, e.g. â€” and â†’?

PHENOMENAL!  As you know, I'm no researcher nor a statistician, but I do have a high-school-level awareness that a study you cite should absolutely support what you say it supports, and each of these 4 examples is easy to understand!

1. A citation that says the *opposite* of the claim it supports
(How crooked is that, for the scientist to do that in the paper??)

2. A credential upgrade -- an open-label trial cited as RCT
(Do they not KNOW the difference?? Or did they just LIE?)

3. A dead-end citation -- the cited paper says nothing of the sort
(I mean, holy CRAP. It's like handing a bouncer a random chunk of plastic and hoping he won't notice it's not a driver's license.)

4. Citing a paper 8 months after it was retracted for being BS
(I'm out of jaw-dropped things to say)

Peter Frishauf you'll love this well documented grotesque failure of the peer review system.

To summarize: in pro-hydroxychloroquine articles TWENTY PERCENT (19.7%) of ALL citations had these "distortions." What a valuable thing for the community to know.

THANK YOU
Hugo Gilles Laura Grace Burt Rasu Susan Susannah Bertalan Andrea Helene Peter
